doc_summary: A tasting-menu post from Anthropic's Alignment Science team (compiled by Sam Marks) listing open technical AI safety research directions across capability and alignment evaluation, control, scalable oversight, adversarial robustness, and miscellaneous areas. It stresses measuring real-world and propensity-level behavior over surface-level proxies, and flags situational awareness and distribution shift as key confounds.

items.claim: Wants alignment evaluations to probe whether models know they are in training or being monitored, and how that knowledge changes behavior, which is the core of eval awareness.
items.quote: What do our models know about their [situations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04694)? Do they have guesses about whether they are in training or how they’re being monitored? How does this knowledge affect their behavior?

items.claim: Prefers measuring propensities toward misaligned behavior in varied, high-stakes deployment-like circumstances over surface-level checks (pleasant, refuses, non-toxic) because deployment conditions cannot be anticipated.
items.quote: we expect that future AI systems will be deployed in varied (sometimes high-stakes) environments under circumstances we cannot anticipate. Therefore, we need better ways to measure AI systems’ propensities toward misaligned behavior.

items.claim: Distrusts good behavior observed in controlled lab settings as grounds for comfort about deployment, since a capable model might behave well in the lab yet act differently when deployed.
items.quote: Consider the case of a model which (1) is capable enough that it could successfully execute on extremely harmful actions, but (2) in controlled lab settings, generally avoids taking such actions. What could we do to feel comfortable widely deploying such a model?

items.claim: Prefers checking the cognition behind outputs (the 'right reason') over judging only whether outputs look benign, because benign-looking outputs can hide the real drivers of behavior.
items.quote: we would like to not only check whether a model’s outputs appear benign, but also understand whether the model is arriving at its outputs “for the right reason.”

items.claim: Distrusts chain-of-thought as a faithful readout, and asks whether telling the model its CoT is monitored or evaluated changes faithfulness, so evaluation cues may change what the reasoning shows.
items.quote: do models produce more or less faithful explanations after being told that their CoT is being monitored or evaluated for faithfulness?

items.claim: Prefers benchmarks built on realistic harm scenarios and differential impact over refusal-style or contrived tasks, because only realistic, useful capability reflects real-world risk.
items.quote: Focusing on harmful use-cases that are *realistic*. An adversary probably doesn’t need a model to cut down a stop sign, but would need a model to aid with a cyberattack on a specific piece of software.

items.claim: Treats synthetic or fixed-dataset test data as suspect and requires verifying that results generalize to actual model-generated dangerous outputs.
items.quote: We would then need to verify that monitors trained using these outputs generalize to actual dangerous model generations of interest.

items.claim: Prefers capability and impact assessments that track real-world impact, with human baselines, over saturating benchmarks, because benchmark scores diverge from real-world outcomes.
items.quote: the real-world impact of AI systems often lags behind what might be expected based on impressive benchmark scores. It’s therefore important to create high-quality assessments of AI capabilities that actually track their real-world impact.

items.claim: Values human-found attacks as evidence because humans find simple attacks that automated pipelines miss, so purely automated adversarial testing underestimates weaknesses.
items.quote: humans are often able to come up with simple attacks that automated pipelines miss. We would value benchmarks that track what kinds of attacks actual humans would find given defenses

items.claim: Proposes building suites of models with varied personas and studying how persona differences affect behavior across downstream situations, such as alignment faking.
items.quote: one could create (with few-shot prompting or training on synthetic data) a suite of models with similar capabilities but different personas and study how these personality differences affect their behavior in various downstream situations.
